_sources.title: Study reveals rising ‘double threat’ of wildfire smoke and heatwaves in Indonesia

1.why: T stands for absolute temperature measured in kelvin.

wrong.a: Celsius is not used in T to the fourth power.
wrong.c: Time is not in this formula.

2.why: Simultaneous smoke and extreme heat stress both heart and lungs.

wrong.b: Smoke does not cool the air down.
wrong.c: Both hazards occur throughout the day.

3.why: Absolute temperature in kelvin is required for power radiation calculations.

wrong.b: Fahrenheit is not standard in physics formulas.

_quiz_pool.question: In P = σ × A × T⁴, what does σ represent?
What is the unit of radiated power P?
If you double the absolute temperature T, radiated power increases by a factor of...
What scale must be used for T in the Stefan-Boltzmann law?
_quiz_pool.explanation: Absolute temperature must be in kelvin.

_quiz_pool.question: Why do heatwaves and wildfire smoke often happen together?
options: Hot dry weather dries out vegetation and sparks fires
_quiz_pool.explanation: Hot, dry conditions create high fire risk and extreme heat.

_quiz_pool.question: What does A stand for in the radiation formula?
_quiz_pool.explanation: A represents the surface area emitting radiation.

safety: no flame, no hot liquids, no mains electricity

cover.title: Wildfire smoke and heatwaves
cover.subtitle: A new study reveals a rising double threat of smoke and extreme heat across Indonesia. Explore how temperatures and radiated power work.
cover.subject: Physics · Radiation
cover.fun_fact: Objects at higher absolute temperature radiate energy proportional to the fourth power of temperature (T⁴).
story.title: The rising double threat in Indonesia
story.lead: A major study in Science Advances shows millions in Indonesia face simultaneous wildfire smoke and heatwaves [1]. Extreme heat and haze strain public health [2].
story.image_caption: Archive photo · VENTZ control panel for heat and smoke vents

stat.2.label: heatwave exposure days per person per year
stat.3.label: estimated excess deaths during peak haze months
story.body_1: Monash University scientists analyzed 20 years of data, revealing a global double threat of wildfire smoke and heatwaves [1]. Indonesia ranks highest in population co-exposure, averaging 101 million people affected annually [1]. Dry conditions and El Niño amplify both hazards, blanketing regions like Central Kalimantan in thick haze [1].
story.body_2: In 2026, millions breathed hazardous air while enduring severe heatwaves, causing hundreds of thousands of acute respiratory infections [1]. Public health experts warn that combining smoke inhalation and thermal stress sharply increases cardiovascular and respiratory risks, especially for vulnerable populations [1].
timeline.1.text: Temperatures rise and dry conditions trigger wildfires.
timeline.2.text: Thick smoke blankets towns and cities across regions.
timeline.3.text: Heatwaves and smoke combine to stress public health.
physics.title: Radiated power and temperature
physics.body_1: Hot objects emit thermal radiation into their surroundings. The total power radiated by a surface depends on its area, its temperature, and fundamental constants.
physics.body_2: In this stretch formula, P is the radiated power in watts, σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, A is the surface area in square metres, and T is the absolute temperature in kelvin.
physics.assumptions: We assume a blackbody emitter with emissivity equal to 1 and uniform surface temperature.
table.note: Higher temperature raises radiated power via T⁴.
graph.title: Radiated power at different temperatures
graph.1.label: 300 K
graph.2.label: 310 K
graph.3.label: 320 K
graph.note: A small rise in absolute temperature causes a large increase in radiated energy.
physics.tip: Because temperature is raised to the fourth power in T⁴, even a slight warming greatly increases thermal radiation.

lab.title: Warmth and radiation test
lab.step_1: Place a dark paper and a light paper near a sunny window for 15 minutes.
lab.step_2: Feel the temperature of both papers carefully with your hand.
lab.step_3: Compare how much heat each paper absorbed from sunlight.
lab.question: Which paper absorbed more radiant energy and felt warmer?
